title: Bike Camping With A Light Phone III – Mitchell Connell
content:
Mitchell Connell chooses connection over connectivity, intention over integration, and looking around over looking down in this thought-provoking review of the Light Phone III. By the end of the review, he was even content to leave it at home. While you might not think a product’s goal is to go unused, that is not entirely the case with this one.

﻿

MapQuest Bike Camping

In June 2011, a small crew of my high school friends and I loaded our bicycles with miscellaneous camping-related things and headed southeast from our homes in Nashville, Tennessee. Our destination was Manchester, where some of our favorite bands were playing Bonnaroo, like Buffalo Springfield, My Morning Jacket, and Beirut. I carried my mother’s Canon AE-1 Program, and my brother carried turn-by-turn directions freshly printed from MapQuest.com.

When we made it emotionally halfway, we set up camp in a field by the road. Three of us slept on a large blue tarp from the local hardware store, and Lane lathered himself in homemade bug spray and strung a hammock between two trees along the property line. By morning, Lane was covered in ticks, while those of us who had slept on the ground couldn’t find a single one.

Sometime during college, bike camping began to change for me. Suddenly, my iPhone could chime whenever Ride with GPS thought I had wandered off-route. I could check my email from my sleeping bag. I could search for the next gas station along the following day’s route. All of this information made traveling much simpler (we had been lost for nearly the entire ride to Bonnaroo), but I began to wonder whether that simplicity came at a cost.

What had once been an exercise in uncertainty and improvisation was becoming another time to manage notifications, battery life, and data. Plus, I couldn’t help wondering what my high school heroes like Matt Segal or Grant Petersen would think of me checking my sleep score at camp or worrying that my iPhone might run out of data.

The Light Phone III

Fast-forward fifteen years and five iPhones. My friend Weston Poling showed me his Light Phone III, a simple cellphone that could text, make calls, manage a calendar, play music and podcasts, provide directions, and not do much else.

I was already familiar with Light Phone. I had owned a Light Phone II, but after one of its buttons broke, it was relegated to the drawer where my old charging cords go to die. Weston’s Light Phone III made me curious again. The screen was better, texting was easier, and the whole device felt like a night-and-day improvement over its predecessor.

I reached out to the folks at Light Phone and asked whether they would send me a loaner to use for a few weeks and take on a camping trip. A few days later, someone emailed me back with a simple response, “Why not?”

Planning the Trip

The premise was simple. A bike camping trip without a smartphone or bike computer. I planned an easy 30-mile round-trip route from downtown Chattanooga to a nearby swimming hole. I have never been particularly good at remembering road names or directions in general, so I kept the ride close to home.

I printed a small map of the full route, along with a zoomed-in map of one particularly tricky section, and laminated both. Just like in high school, I attached them to the stem of my bike with a binder clip.

Once the route was settled, I spent a somewhat significant amount of time typing out the trip details, then copied and pasted them into messages to about ten friends. Over the next few days, my phone chimed as people joined the trip or let me know they couldn’t make it. Before I knew it, the weekend had arrived.

Using the Phone on the Trip

The first thing I noticed while riding without a head unit or Strava was how slowly I was riding. I guess when I can’t see my speed, and I’m not tracking the ride to publish on the internet, I suddenly don’t care that I’m going eight miles per hour. Besides, the whole ride that day was fifteen miles. Who cares if it takes two hours?

The Light Phone III is also really fun to shoot video with. I wish I could press a single button and immediately open the video interface, but instead it takes about four taps to start recording. Still, the video quality is really nice. It reminds me of footage from point-and-shoot cameras made between 2005 and 2010. I found myself taking lots of short clips while riding and hanging around camp.

There isn’t an official campsite where we were headed, and there are several similar-looking pull-offs along the steady climb at the end of the route. It sounds kind of silly, but not knowing how much longer a climb will last feels very psychologically different. Instead of watching the distance tick down on a screen, I had to keep my head on a swivel and look for the graffiti that marked our pull-off. I was certainly paying more attention than I would have been if I were simply rolling along and waiting for my Wahoo to tell me when to stop.

We arrived just before dark and set up a humble camp on the sloped banks of the creek. I texted my wife to let her know we had made it, and then we headed to bed. The next morning we woke up early, and Thor headed off to fish. My friend Jon Jon had brought snorkeling gear, so after coffee we walked downstream to look for fish. Once we were all properly chilled by the cold water, we packed up our gear and headed back toward town.

The whole trip took less than twenty-four hours and barely carried us beyond the edge of the city, but it still felt like an adventure. It’s always nice to be reminded that bike camping doesn’t have to be ambitious or complicated. Sometimes all it takes is fifteen miles, a place to sleep, and a reason to leave your phone in your pocket.

Not Always Available: How the Light Phone Changed My Day-to-Day Life

The first change I noticed was my relationship with email. Suddenly, I couldn’t check every five minutes to see whether someone had gotten back to me. It felt strange for the first few days, but eventually I settled into it. Now, I have a much healthier relationship with work communication, and I genuinely believe I’ve gotten better at responding to people. Instead of checking constantly and replying sporadically, I sit down, focus, and deal with my inbox all at once.

The second change was directions. I’ve lived in Chattanooga for four years, so I know my way around pretty well. The Light Phone has a directions app that works well enough, but I’ve started carrying a small notebook and writing down directions whenever I’m headed somewhere unfamiliar, like picking up something from Facebook Marketplace. This has been absolutely lovely. It keeps me engaged while I’m on the road and has helped me discover and remember new pockets of the city.

My relationship with podcasts and music has changed too. The Light Phone has a great podcast app and a functional music app, but using them feels very different from having immediate access to an endless stream of music and commentary. For whatever reason, I’ve mostly stopped listening to anything while riding my bicycle or running. For me, that adds up to seven to nine hours each week that now feel entirely different. I notice where I am. Sometimes I’m just bored. It’s nice.

A Mini Light Phone Review

The Light Phone III is a beautiful object. It has a reassuring weight in your hand and feels extremely well built. Call quality is good, and the screen is bright and easy to read. Texting on the OLED screen is noticeably less accurate and responsive than typing on an iPhone’s buttery-smooth screen, but you get used to it. You will probably find yourself texting less and calling more, simply because calling is easier.

The calendar app syncs with the major calendar services, and the phone plays a pleasant chime when it reminds you that you need to be somewhere in half an hour. The hotspot works well too. When you genuinely need the internet, you can connect another device, like a laptop, and get online.

I also really like the camera. Rather than trying to compete with modern smartphones, Light Phone went in a different direction. The photos and videos remind me of a Canon PowerShot from the 2000s. The camera feels nostalgic without seeming like a gimmick, and I absolutely love the video quality.

The Light Phone III is not all roses, though. For one, it’s really expensive. The price recently increased to $899, which is a lot for my bike shop salary. I am thankful that Light Phone sent me a demo because I am not sure I could spend $899 while I still have an older iPhone that works perfectly well, even if I sometimes feel like it is slowly killing me.

The music app is also terrible. I know most people don’t use MP3s anymore, but I do! The app displays every song you have downloaded in one continuous list, arranged in the order you added them. There is no useful way to browse by artist or album. At the very least, the songs should be arranged alphabetically and organized into folders.

My other major concern is water resistance. The phone is designed to be repairable, but that comes at the expense of waterproofing. As someone who commutes by bicycle, I worry about carrying an $899 phone in my pocket when an unexpected rainstorm rolls in.

Final thoughts

Even with all of these complaints, I love the Light Phone III. Giving up my smartphone has been one of the most meaningful changes I’ve made in the last few years, and I highly recommend trying it for yourself.

Last weekend, I went on a canoe trip with my wife and brother. Worried that my phone might get wet, I left it at home. I spent two days on the river and never once wished I had brought a cellphone with me. Maybe the best review I can give the Light Phone is this: it helped turn my phone into something I’m happy to leave behind.

Pros

  • Intentionally designed to be used less often with greater intention
  • Stellar build quality
  • Camera has lots of character

Cons

  • Podcast and music playing function is underbaked
  • Waterproofing is questionable
  • Very expensive for what it is

See the Light Phone III.
